headings.title: Introduction to Bites and Stings in Nursing Care
headings.content: Bites and stings are common encounters in nursing practice across Nigeria, ranging from mild local irritation to life-threatening medical emergencies. Nurses must understand that environmental factors, occupational hazards such as farming, and geographic distribution heavily influence the prevalence and types of bites and stings patients present with. Venomous snakes, scorpions, spiders, bees, wasps, and stray animals contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality if improperly managed. In Nigerian healthcare settings, rapid clinical assessment and prompt administration of first aid are critical nursing responsibilities. Nurses serve as the frontline evaluators who determine the severity of envenomation or tissue trauma, initiate supportive therapies, and educate communities on prevention. Recognizing the systemic and local manifestations of various bites ensures timely interventions that prevent severe complications, including necrosis, acute kidney injury, and fatal anaphylaxis. Comprehensive nursing care involves not only immediate resuscitation and symptom management but also thorough documentation, wound surveillance, and emotional support for distressed patients and their families.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Types of Venoms and Toxins
headings.content: Venoms and toxins injected through animal bites and insect stings are complex biochemical mixtures composed of proteins, enzymes, and peptides that target various physiological systems in the human body. Understanding pathophysiology helps nursing students anticipate specific clinical manifestations. Cytotoxins, commonly found in certain snake venoms, cause localized tissue destruction, cell lysis, and severe necrosis by breaking down cellular membranes. Hemotoxins disrupt the body's normal coagulation cascade, leading to severe hemorrhage, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), or spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes. Neurotoxins interfere with neuromuscular transmission by blocking acetylcholine receptors or affecting nerve conduction, which can rapidly result in descending paralysis, cranial nerve deficits, and respiratory failure. In contrast, insect venoms from bees, wasps, and ants primarily trigger IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reactions, releasing massive amounts of histamine, leukotrienes, and cytokines that cause vasodilation, bronchospasm, and systemic capillary leak. Animal bites from mammals often introduce polymicrobial flora, including Pasteurella species and anaerobes, directly into deep tissue planes, rapidly precipitating localized cellulitis and deep-seated wound infections if not adequately scrubbed and monitored.

headings.title: Assessment and Triage of Affected Patients
headings.content: Effective triage and assessment of patients presenting with bites and stings require a systematic nursing approach using the ABCDE framework (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure). Triage nurses must immediately identify red flags such as stridor, hypotension, altered mental status, active bleeding, or rapidly spreading edema. The history should focus on the time of the incident, the specific creature involved if known, the geographical location of the event, and the progression of symptoms since the bite or sting occurred. Physical examination must carefully evaluate the local site for fang marks, puncture wounds, erythema, swelling, warmth, and signs of localized tissue ischemia or necrosis. Systemic assessments should monitor vital signs continuously, checking for tachycardia, tachypnea, oxygen desaturation, and falling blood pressure that indicate systemic envenomation, shock, or developing anaphylaxis. Laboratory investigations ordered promptly by the interprofessional team often include complete blood counts, coagulation profiles (such as whole blood clotting time), and renal function tests. Accurate baseline documentation allows nurses to track symptom progression and evaluate the effectiveness of administered emergency treatments over time.

headings.title: Management of Insect Stings and Localized Reactions
headings.content: Insect stings from bees, wasps, hornets, and fire ants cause localized pain, redness, swelling, and mild pruritus in most individuals. The immediate nursing priority upon presentation is to gently remove any remaining stinger by scraping it off horizontally with a rigid card or fingernail rather than using tweezers, which can squeeze more venom into the skin sac. Once the stinger is removed, the nurse should wash the affected area thoroughly with soap and clean water to prevent secondary bacterial contamination. Applying a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth helps reduce local edema, pain, and inflammatory mediator release by causing vasoconstriction. Elevation of the affected extremity can further minimize swelling, especially if the sting is located on a hand or foot. Over-the-counter or prescribed topical calamine lotion, oral antihistamines, and mild analgesics can be administered to alleviate itching and discomfort. Nurses must closely observe the patient for at least 30 minutes following an insect sting to ensure localized symptoms do not progress into a systemic or severe allergic reaction.

headings.title: Emergency Care for Snakebites and Animal Bites
headings.content: Snakebites and severe animal bites require urgent, highly structured emergency nursing interventions. For snakebites, the primary goals are to slow systemic venom absorption, prevent life-threatening complications, and prepare for antivenom administration. The nurse must keep the patient calm and immobilize the affected limb in a neutral, dependent or slightly elevated position, avoiding traditional harmful practices such as tourniquet application, incisions, or black stone usage. If the bite is from an elapid snake causing neurotoxic symptoms, a pressure immobilization bandage may be indicated per specific protocol. Intravenous access must be secured promptly, and baseline blood samples drawn. Antivenom is the definitive treatment for systemic envenomation and should be administered under close clinical supervision, with emergency resuscitation equipment and epinephrine readily available to manage potential hypersensitivity reactions. For mammalian animal bites, such as dog or cat bites, immediate high-pressure irrigation with sterile normal saline is crucial to wash out debris and bacteria. Broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis must be administered promptly, and wound closure is often delayed to prevent trapping bacteria within deep tissues.

headings.title: Recognizing and Treating Anaphylactic Shock
headings.content: Anaphylactic shock is a severe, rapidly progressive, multi-system IgE-mediated allergic reaction triggered by insect stings, animal proteins, or other allergens. Nurses must rapidly recognize early signs of anaphylaxis, which include generalized urticaria, angioedema, intense pruritus, anxiety, and a feeling of impending doom, quickly progressing to respiratory distress with wheezing, laryngeal edema, and profound cardiovascular collapse with hypotension. The single most important, life-saving intervention is the immediate intramuscular administration of adrenaline (epinephrine) into the anterolateral thigh, as delay can be fatal. Nurses should place the patient in a recumbent position with lower extremities elevated unless respiratory distress is severe, in which case a comfortable sitting position may be allowed. High-flow oxygen must be delivered via a non-rebreather mask to address hypoxemia. Secondary emergency interventions include establishing large-bore intravenous access for rapid fluid resuscitation with normal saline, and administering adjunct medications such as H1 and H2 antihistamines, nebulized beta-agonists, and systemic corticosteroids to prevent biphasic reactions. Continuous hemodynamic and respiratory monitoring is mandatory until the patient is completely stabilized.

headings.title: Complications, Secondary Infections, and Wound Care
headings.content: Patients who survive the initial phase of bites and stings remain at significant risk for various local and systemic complications. Cytotoxic venoms and deep animal bite wounds often lead to extensive tissue necrosis, compartment syndrome, and severe secondary bacterial infections including cellulitis, abscess formation, and osteomyelitis. Nurses play a crucial role in meticulous wound care, which involves aseptic dressing changes, monitoring for purulent discharge, foul odors, or spreading erythema, and assessing distal pulses, capillary refill, and motor function in affected limbs. Tetanus immunization status must be verified for every patient, and a booster dose administered if their vaccination history is incomplete or greater than five years for contaminated wounds. In cases of severe systemic envenomation, nurses must closely monitor urine output hourly via indwelling catheters to detect early signs of acute kidney injury or rhabdomyolysis resulting from myoglobinuria. Appropriate pain management, nutritional support, and physical therapy referrals are integrated into the nursing care plan to promote optimal tissue healing and functional recovery.

headings.title: Patient Education and Prevention Strategies
headings.content: Patient education and community prevention strategies are essential components of comprehensive nursing care to reduce the recurrence of bites and stings, particularly in endemic rural and agricultural areas in Nigeria. Nurses should educate patients and communities on environmental modifications, such as clearing tall grass and bushes around dwellings, sealing entry points in homes, and avoiding walking barefoot at night or handling snakes without proper protective gear. Agricultural workers should be advised to wear thick protective boots, gloves, and long trousers while farming. For individuals with known severe insect allergies, nurses must provide thorough instruction on how to recognize early symptoms of anaphylaxis and how to properly use an epinephrine auto-injector. Patients should be taught to carry their emergency medication at all times and wear a medical alert bracelet. Education should also emphasize avoiding dangerous traditional first-aid practices for snakebites, encouraging immediate presentation to a certified healthcare facility instead. Empowering communities with this knowledge significantly decreases morbidity and mortality associated with environmental envenomations.
